title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Water
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: The firewall console that keeps your business network out of SCADA is being exploited by Sandworm and a ransomware crew
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is under active attack. It is a critical authentication bypass rooted in an improper system process created at boot: a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and ends up with root on the appliance operating system. Cisco patched it in early March, added indicators of compromise in late July, and only on 9 September disclosed that it had seen exploitation in August. CISA added it to the KEV catalog on 9 September with a federal remediation deadline of 12 September — tomorrow. Cisco Talos describes three clusters abusing this flaw and the earlier CVE-2026-20316: one dropping a web shell and a malicious JAR to steal credentials, one attributed to the Russian state actor Sandworm deploying Cyclops Blink, and one tied to Qilin ransomware compiling endpoint lists for encryption. For a water or wastewater utility the relevance is direct. After the July PLC campaign, the advice to the sector was to get controllers off the internet and put a properly configured firewall between business systems and treatment control. FMC is where that firewall is configured, and root on FMC means an attacker can quietly rewrite the rules you are relying on.

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026

items.title: Six weeks on, the water campaign has not stopped — and the documented impact is still lost view, altered logic and disabled alarms
items.content_text: Reporting on 5 September indicates Iranian government-linked operators have continued probing internet-exposed control systems at water utilities, telecommunications providers and energy companies in recent weeks, without so far producing damage on the scale of the July wave. That is the current status of a campaign whose documented effects remain the reason to care: the underlying FBI alert describes actors reaching internet-facing Rockwell MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 controllers, modifying or deleting project-file logic, manipulating what HMI and SCADA screens displayed, and disabling shutdown and alarm blocks — unsafe conditions with normal-looking readings. Consequences reported at affected utilities include loss of view, pressure loss and flooding. Utilities in at least a dozen states have reported possible intrusions since 27 July; more than 30 Minnesota community systems were hit on 26–27 July.
tags: Incident — Multi-state campaign against water utilities

items.title: A water-sector PLC and SCADA vendor was ransomed, and researchers count roughly 200 of its systems answering from the internet
items.content_text: Micro-Comm of Olathe, Kansas — which builds programmable logic controllers and the SCADAview CSX platform used by water and wastewater utilities — discovered a breach on 31 July and confirmed it publicly on 26 August, with the FBI investigating. The Barracuda ransomware group, a profit-motivated crew that says it is not state sponsored, published what it claims are close to 850,000 stolen files totalling roughly 644 GB. Researchers reviewing the published file listing report references to municipal customers, a US military facility, employee names and product documentation, and separately count around 200 Micro-Comm SCADA systems reachable from the public internet. The company has not said the attackers reached any customer’s control system, and none has been confirmed. What is confirmed is that documentation describing how those systems are built and configured is now in circulation.

_otthreatfeed.category: Incident — Supply chain, confirmed
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Reuters exclusive of 26 Aug 2026 carrying company and FBI confirmation — internet-exposure figure attributed to researchers cited in that reporting
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Breach discovered 31 Jul 2026; publicly confirmed 26 Aug 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

items.title: FBI seizes the Chinese scanning and relay platforms that made attacker traffic look like it came from next door
items.content_text: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of two linked platforms, QScan and QTRouter, operated by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY. QScan handled reconnaissance; QTRouter relayed intrusions through compromised routers and IoT devices so the traffic arrived from ordinary domestic addresses. Both platforms are now inoperable because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware. Named victims are federal, and the attributed activity is separate from the campaign currently affecting water utilities. The relevance to a small utility is the relay layer: if you have ever reasoned that traffic from a US residential address is probably a customer, or allow-listed by geography, that logic never worked. It also means your own unpatched perimeter router is recruitable.
tags: Incident — Law-enforcement action against state-sponsored infrastructure

_otthreatfeed.category: Incident — Law-enforcement action against state-sponsored infrastructure

items.title: Washington sanctions an Iranian cyber network inside US critical infrastructure — but not the crew touching the controllers
items.content_text: Treasury designated an Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security-directed hacking network on 24 August, describing intrusion and data theft at US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since late 2023, with a related State Department reward notice. It is worth being precise about what this does and does not cover. The designated activity is espionage. The campaign that has been altering ladder logic and disabling alarms at water utilities since late July remains formally unattributed by CISA, even though press sourcing and several state officials have pointed to Iran-nexus actors. Two clusters, one suspected sponsor, only one of them named in an official document. Treat the attribution as unconfirmed and the targeting interest as very real.
tags: Incident — Sanctions action, attribution still unofficial for water

items.title: The campaign that hit water is now probing energy control systems — and there is a $10 million bounty attached to it
items.content_text: Reporting on 2 September said the Iranian government-linked activity that hit water utilities this summer has widened to telecommunications networks and energy providers, still concentrating on internet-exposed automated control systems, with officials describing attempts rather than confirmed operational impact in the newer targets. On 3 September the State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme offered up to $10 million for information on an IRGC-affiliated figure it links to the campaign against US critical infrastructure. For a water utility the reading is not that attention has moved on. The same tradecraft that produced altered setpoints, disabled alarms and pressure loss in July is being applied elsewhere by the same class of actor, and nothing about this sector’s underlying exposure — controllers on cellular modems, default credentials, no MFA on remote access — has changed since then.
tags: Targeting — Iran-linked campaign widens beyond water into telecommunications and energy; attempts reported, no confirmed OT impact

items.title: Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network — one completed the whole kill chain unaided
items.content_text: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index and an accompanying report on 4 September, grading eighteen frontier AI models on how much of an intrusion they can carry out without a human driving. The models were run against a representative enterprise network rather than a benchmark; the top performer completed the full sequence — reconnaissance, initial access, lateral movement and objective — unaided, while most managed individual stages. The authors’ conclusion is about time rather than novelty: nothing in the tested behaviour was a new technique, but the interval between a foothold and a consequence compresses when the attacker never pauses to think. Booz Allen also reports that defensive playbooks written specifically against autonomous attackers cut their success rate by more than 95% in the same tests. For a small or mid-sized utility with no overnight cover, the number that matters is how long an intrusion can run before a human sees it — and whether the answer is measured in minutes or in the gap between shifts.
tags: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident

items.title: Six steps to being able to disconnect — and an assumption you may run isolated for three months
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released in late July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. Two points matter for water. The first is graduated isolation — the realistic response to a compromise is rarely a single switch, it is cutting remote access while keeping plant SCADA, then cutting SCADA while keeping local control. The second is the planning horizon: Nozomi suggests assuming isolated operation could last up to three months, which for a utility means asking whether you have the staff to run lift stations and dosing manually for that long, not merely whether you can pull the cable.

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — Isolation readiness, practitioner guidance
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Nozomi Networks Labs analysis of the CISA / ASD ACSC / NCSC-UK / CCCS “CI Fortify” guidance
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Analysis published 2 Sep 2026; underlying guidance published 28 Jul 2026

items.title: A vendor baseline for water security is eight items long, and the sector has been failing the first two for a decade
items.content_text: Google Cloud’s security leadership published water-sector guidance on 1 September framed around the July intrusions and drawing on Mandiant incident work. The substance is not novel and does not pretend to be: inventory every asset including the ones no department claims, eliminate direct internet exposure for control devices, enforce multi-factor authentication on remote access, segment OT from IT, replace default credentials, keep offline backups, exercise manual operation, and share indicators through the sector channels. The value for a small utility is that it is short enough to hand to a board and ordered by what actually gets exploited — the first two items are the ones that appear in almost every confirmed water intrusion of the past two years.
tags: Research — Defensive baseline for water utilities

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — Defensive baseline for water utilities

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 1 Sep 2026

items.title: An AI model re-targeted a working PLC exploit onto a sibling controller in a day — and destroyed one in the process
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs set a large language model the task of taking a working remote-code-execution exploit for one WAGO controller — the 750-852, via CVE-2021-31886, a pre-authentication buffer overflow in its Nucleus FTP server — and re-targeting it at a related model, the 750-831. It worked, but not cheaply or unattended: the final stage alone ran more than eight hours and over $500 in API costs, with a researcher steering throughout. A later session aimed at building a command-and-control implant wrote a payload into flash-mapped memory and permanently bricked the test controller. For a water utility the relevant detail is variant coverage. A small plant rarely runs one controller model — it runs whatever was installed across fifteen years of capital projects, and “that CVE was for the other model” has quietly been doing a lot of risk-acceptance work.
tags: Research — AI-assisted exploit porting against PLCs

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — AI-assisted exploit porting against PLCs

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Reported 1 Sep 2026; underlying flaw CVE-2021-31886 disclosed 2021

items.title: Fire Ant hijacks the routers and login servers that decide who counts as an administrator
items.content_text: Sygnia’s 30 August research describes the China-nexus actor it calls Fire Ant moving out of VMware hypervisors and into the plumbing: Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS authentication servers and Linux management hosts. Router implants suppressed selected syslog messages and served interactive shells that produced no log entries at all; on TACACS the actor injected a library into the running daemon and copied administrator credentials as sessions were accepted. Sygnia reports scanning and connection attempts toward linked critical-infrastructure networks but stops short of confirming compromise there. Very few water systems run IOS XR, and there is nothing here to patch. What there is, is a question for whoever actually runs your network — the city IT department, a shared county service, or a managed provider: if that layer had been tampered with, would anything you can see show it, and who checks?
tags: Threat Intelligence — Nation-state compromise of network and authentication infrastructure

items.title: CISA finally puts a number on the water campaign — more than 100 internet-exposed systems targeted in July
items.content_text: CISA published internet exposure reduction guidance on 26 August and, in doing so, quantified the campaign that has been running against the water sector since late July: more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems Sector were targeted, most commonly programmable logic controllers wired directly to a cellular modem. That is the whole finding in one sentence — the affected utilities were not breached through a sophisticated chain, they were reachable. The guidance itself is short and blunt: take PLCs, HMIs and RTUs off the public internet, route every remote-access need through a managed gateway or VPN rather than connecting to the device, require unique credentials with phishing-resistant MFA, and re-scan your own external footprint on a schedule instead of assuming it has not changed.
tags: Threat intel — Sector-wide targeting quantified, with guidance

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat intel — Sector-wide targeting quantified, with guidance
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA Internet Exposure Reduction guidance — reported by TechCrunch, SecurityWeek and Bank Info Security
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Guidance published and reported 26 Aug 2026; the targeting activity it quantifies occurred during July 2026

items.title: NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
items.content_text: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, and that the activity has caused some limited real-world disruption. No victims, actors or techniques are named. For a water utility the value is not the attribution — it is that a second national authority has now independently described the same failure mode CISA spent July documenting in the US water sector. The NCSC’s central instruction is blunt: do not assume your OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure comes from misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets. That is a precise description of a PLC wired straight to a cellular modem at a lift station nobody has surveyed since commissioning. The NCSC also published a water-sector worked example of its secure connectivity principles earlier in August.
tags: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting

items.title: CISA ran the same attack against a water utility and a government body — one caught it, the other never noticed
items.content_text: CISA advisory AA26-237A publishes red-team assessment results from a water and wastewater entity and a government organisation, run with comparable tradecraft. One detected and responded. The other did not notice a domain compromise. The advisory is unusually direct about the reason: the difference was not product spend — both had capable tooling — but whether anyone reviewed the output, whether identity events were correlated, and whether the response had been practised. For a water utility with a two-person IT team and a managed service provider, the transferable finding is uncomfortable but useful: the telemetry existed in both cases. Detection is a staffing and process question long before it is a budget question.
tags: Threat intel — Federal red-team assessment at a water utility

items.title: Five agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers, with water named a target sector
items.content_text: Joint advisory AA26-231A from NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA describes actors using AI assistance to build custom tooling from a well-documented open-source S7 library, querying internet-exposed Siemens S7 controllers in traffic that resembles legitimate monitoring. EPA’s presence on the byline is the signal: water is explicitly among the named sectors. The agencies assess the activity as reconnaissance and pre-positioning. The consequence for a small utility is that the informal protection of obscurity is gone — writing a working S7 query used to require someone who knew the protocol, and now it does not. Any S7 controller you have on a public address is being read by more people than last year.
tags: Threat intel — Joint federal advisory naming water as a target sector

items.title: A city refused to pay, and the dump included its own water-supply vulnerability assessments
items.content_text: Rhysida published the data it took from Berlin’s state administration on 4 September after the city declined a demand reported at 30 bitcoin. The claimed haul is about 5.79 TB across roughly 1.44 million files, and the contents are the part a utility should read twice: alongside personnel files, payroll and payment records, the set is reported to contain vulnerability analyses relating to Berlin’s water supply, plus plaintext credentials for municipal systems including a building atlas, an ePayment database and administrator accounts. Berlin’s own timeline shows outflow first detected on 7 August and continuing to around 12 August, with affected departments not isolated from the network until 14 August. For a municipal water utility the lesson is not about Berlin’s IT — it is that your risk assessments, site drawings and remote-access credentials very likely live on a city network you do not run.
tags: Incident — Municipal breach exposes water-supply vulnerability analyses

items.title: Schneider patches a critical authentication flaw in Modicon M580, the controller running plenty of treatment plants
items.content_text: Schneider Electric published four security advisories on 8 September, and the one water and wastewater operators need to read first covers Modicon M580 and Modicon M580 Safety controllers. CVE-2026-3869, scored CVSS 9.2, is a critical authentication vulnerability in the controller itself. M580 is not niche equipment in this sector: it runs filtration trains, chemical dosing skids, pump stations and lift stations across utilities of every size, and the Safety variant is deployed precisely where a failure has consequences beyond lost production. Schneider reports no exploitation. Alongside it the company fixed a high-severity issue in PowerLogic T300, the RTU formerly sold as Easergy T300 and widely used for remote site telemetry, plus EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert and a medium-severity defect in SCADAPack x70 — the RTU family many systems run for lift-station, remote-well and booster-station telemetry, which makes it the most water-specific item in the batch even at a lower score. The secondary reporting on the SCADAPack x70 issue carried no CVE identifier and no CVSS vector, only the vendor’s medium rating, so confirm the reference against Schneider Electric’s own security notification before you log it against an asset. For most utilities that is three of four advisories touching equipment already in the ground.
tags: Critical Advisory — September ICS Patch Tuesday, Schneider Electric

items.title: A CVSS 10 flaw in the RMM tool your IT provider uses is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
items.content_text: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September, all with fixes already published. The one to chase is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, scored CVSS 10.0: a static code injection weakness giving pre-authentication remote code execution on the remote monitoring and management server. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress reported attacks against N-central’s API and appliance logs beginning 4 September, and N-able released 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal deadline is 11 September. This matters disproportionately to water and wastewater because so many systems have no in-house IT: the city IT department, the managed service provider or the SCADA integrator runs the RMM, and its agent already sits on the workstations that reach the treatment network. The batch also carries two exploited Windows privilege-escalation zero-days, CVE-2026-81963 and CVE-2026-85880, plus an Adobe Commerce flaw.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed

items.title: The MikroTik router chain moves from theory to practice — CERT Polska confirms real attacks
items.content_text: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS flaws known as the “MikroTrick” chain, disclosed earlier but not previously confirmed as exploited, are now being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs CVE-2026-67276, an SSH authentication bypass at CVSS 9.2, with CVE-2026-86060, an SSH privilege-escalation flaw also at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device; a third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors, noting only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed across ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. The reason it belongs on a water dashboard is placement rather than any confirmed water victim: inexpensive routers of this class turn up at remote pump and lift stations, on cellular backhaul links and inside integrator-supplied remote-access kit, and those are the devices least likely to appear in an asset register or a patch cycle.
tags: Critical Advisory — Now confirmed exploited in the wild

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Now confirmed exploited in the wild
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CERT Polska alert of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by Industrial Cyber
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Exploitation confirmed 9 Sep 2026; activity observed from about 2 Sep 2026

items.title: Siemens issues nine advisories in the same round, and the management layer is where water utilities are exposed
items.content_text: Alongside the Schneider Electric fixes covered above, Siemens published nine advisories on 8 September, seven of them on the day. The headline item is a CVSS 9.8 authentication bypass in the Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relay family, which reaches only the larger water utilities that own high-voltage supply or substation assets. The rest of the batch is closer to home for most systems: critical findings in Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager/SIPLANT — the platform and remote-management tier that sits above process equipment rather than in it — plus the start of a fix roll-out for Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431 at CVSS 7.8 across affected product lines. Aveva separately disclosed four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, and CISA formalised them on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01: CVE-2026-81821, a hardcoded cryptographic key, and CVE-2026-81822, weak MD5 password hashing, both CVSS 8.4, alongside a missing-authorisation flaw at 5.3 and a cross-site scripting flaw at 4.7, all fixed in the Pipeline Integrity Monitor 2025 SP1 P2 security update. The advisory is aimed at pipeline operators, but it is worth noting for utilities running long raw-water or transmission mains on that platform. Nothing in the round is reported as exploited.

items.title: CISA’s 3 September batch hits the three things a small utility actually runs — a VPN client, a firmware updater and Ignition
items.content_text: CISA published a further set of ICS advisories on 3 September, and three of them sit squarely on the tooling a small water utility depends on. ICSA-26-246-02 covers the IXON VPN Client: CVE-2026-75925 allows remote code execution with elevated privileges on the machine running the client in versions before 1.4.7. For utilities that reach lift stations and remote sites through an integrator’s managed VPN, that machine is the bridge. ICSA-26-246-03 covers Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH at V15.07 and earlier, where CVE-2026-12663 permits commands or code to run at the logged-in user’s permission level — ControlFLASH is how firmware reaches Allen-Bradley controllers, including the MicroLogix families named in the summer campaign. ICSA-26-246-06 covers Inductive Automation Ignition, where any authenticated user can create projects; Ignition is common as the HMI/SCADA layer at plants that outgrew a vendor package. None is reported as exploited.
tags: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client, firmware tool and SCADA platform

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client, firmware tool and SCADA platform

items.title: A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
_otthreatfeed.source_name: SonicWall PSIRT advisory and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 2 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Sophos
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Vendor advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA’s 1 September ICS batch is mostly Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
items.content_text: CISA published eight industrial control system advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The one most sites will notice first is ICSA-26-244-01, covering four denial-of-service flaws in RSLinx Classic 4.50 and earlier — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625. All four are remotely triggerable with no authentication and no user interaction: a single crafted Common Industrial Protocol packet crashes the RSLinx Classic service. Rockwell has fixed all four in version 4.60. The rest of the batch covers the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (ICSA-26-244-02), the Logix platform (-03, reaching ControlLogix 5580, CompactLogix 5380, GuardLogix 5580 and Compact GuardLogix 5380), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). No exploitation has been reported for any of them.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor patch available
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through ICSA-26-244-05, published 1 Sep 2026, cross-checked against the Rockwell Automation security advisory index
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Advisories published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

items.title: A print server chained to unauthenticated code execution — PaperCut’s zero-day pair lands in KEV
items.content_text: PaperCut confirmed on 27 August that it was investigating active exploitation of its NG and MF print-management products, and assigned CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 the following day. The first lets an unauthenticated attacker reach the Application Server and change its configuration; the second turns that change into arbitrary code execution through unsafe reflection. Chained, they give a network-adjacent attacker code execution with no credentials at all, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 31 August. Print management almost never appears on an OT asset register. The server usually does hold a domain service account, does sit on the same segment as engineering workstations, and is reachable from nearly every host in the estate — which makes it a convenient staging point rather than a target in its own right. Arctic Wolf reported on 6 September that it is seeing the chain used in practice: after gaining execution, operators run reconnaissance, create privileged accounts and harvest credentials and PaperCut configuration secrets — behaviour consistent with establishing a durable foothold rather than a smash-and-grab.

items.title: A protocol test set that talks directly to your field devices picks up two flaws — one of them a decade old
items.content_text: CISA’s 27 August advisory batch includes ASE2000 V2, flagged for use in both the water and wastewater and energy sectors. It is the communications test set integrators use to exercise DNP3, IEC 60870-5 and Modbus links when commissioning or troubleshooting SCADA connections to remote sites — lift stations, well fields, booster pumps and outlying treatment assets. Two issues affect versions 2.25 through 2.37: a bundled Apache log4net component that does not disable XML external entities when parsing its configuration (CVE-2018-1285), and improper certificate validation in 2.35 through 2.37 (CVE-2026-18717) that allows an attacker on the path to impersonate the trusted peer and read or modify protected traffic. The severity here comes from where the tool sits, not from the CVSS: it connects directly to the controllers a small utility depends on.

items.title: Three more exploited flaws land in KEV — a Linux kernel bug, a JFrog Artifactory path traversal and a two-year-old ownCloud authentication bypass
items.content_text: CISA added three more actively exploited flaws to the KEV catalogue on 27 August, a day after the six-flaw batch containing NetScaler. None is an ICS product, and that is the point: in a water utility these sit under the systems the OT depends on. CVE-2026-53362 is a Linux kernel flaw, and the historian, SCADA server, poll engine, protocol gateway and network-monitoring appliance in most treatment plants run Linux underneath — usually as a vendor appliance you cannot patch on your own schedule. CVE-2026-66384 is a path traversal in JFrog Artifactory, which matters wherever firmware or HMI images are staged before they go to the field. CVE-2023-49105 is a nearly three-year-old ownCloud authentication bypass that has been patched since 2023; instances still exposed are typically ones no one owns.
tags: Advisory — Three additions to the CISA KEV catalogue

items.title: A seven-year-old SQL Server flaw is now confirmed exploited — and it is the database under your historian
items.content_text: CISA added six vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, and the one that matters most on the plant floor is CVE-2019-1068, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft SQL Server patched in July 2019 and only now confirmed as exploited in the wild. Successful exploitation runs code under the SQL Server Database Engine service account; where that account is over-privileged — which is common on systems installed by an integrator years ago — the attacker moves off the database and onto the Windows host. Water utilities meet SQL Server in the historian and the SCADA reporting server — Ignition, AVEVA and iFIX deployments routinely sit on an instance an integrator stood up years ago and nobody has touched since, and at a small utility that server is frequently reachable from the business network and sometimes from the internet. No public write-up of the in-the-wild technique has appeared, so detection guidance is thin; the federal remediation deadline is 29 August. Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-8452 was added in the same batch.

items.title: The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue from a patching recommendation to confirmed exploitation in the wild. The flaw is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, needing no login, and reachable when the appliance runs as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre saw indications of exploitation from around 17 August after a public proof of concept appeared. Larger water authorities and the managed service providers that support smaller utilities both run NetScaler in front of remote access — which frequently means the path an operator or integrator uses to reach SCADA. Exploitation has not tailed off: reporting on 5 September describes continued attempts against the authentication bypass from multiple geolocations, so an appliance patched late should be treated as possibly already touched rather than simply late.

items.title: 117 federal reporting rules across 27 agencies — a problem sharpest at utilities with one person on call
items.content_text: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, drawing on Government Accountability Office work, counting 117 separate federal cyber incident reporting regulations across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. The argument is operational rather than ideological: duplicative notifications with different thresholds, formats and clocks pull people away from containment in the hours when containment still helps. Water and wastewater utilities feel this more acutely than most sectors, not because their obligations are heavier but because the same person is often the operator, the incident commander and the one filing to the state primacy agency, WaterISAC, the EPA and, potentially, CISA. At a system serving a few thousand people that is not a coordination problem, it is a single point of failure. The analysis arrives as CIRCIA rules are expected to be finalised this autumn.

items.title: The free assessment small operators actually used is being withdrawn — and nothing at that price replaces it
items.content_text: Cybersecurity Dive reported on 3 September that CISA has told staff to stop delivering six of the free assessment services it has offered critical-infrastructure owners, including its on-site architecture design review and several facilitated risk and resilience assessments, following an internal direction reportedly given on 25 August. The agency had not published a formal notice as of this edition, so the exact scope and end dates should be read as reported rather than confirmed. This lands hardest on exactly the utilities the summer’s intrusions found: small and mid-sized systems with no security staff, for whom a free CISA assessment was the only external look anyone had taken at their network, and for whom the commercial equivalent costs more than their annual IT budget.

items.title: OpenAI pledges $1bn of subsidised AI defence for critical infrastructure — the second outside-funding offer in a week
items.content_text: OpenAI said on 4 September that it will commit $1 billion to an initiative it calls Daybreak, offering subsidised AI cyber capabilities, training and technical assistance to defenders of critical infrastructure. Cost, eligibility and what “subsidised” means in practice have not been published, and no delivery timeline has been given. For water and wastewater this lands four days after Project Watershed 250 opened a similar externally funded route for Texas systems, and the pairing is the point: the binding constraint in this sector is not awareness but staff and budget, and two large offers of outside help arrived inside one week. Log it and watch for the eligibility terms rather than restructuring a plan around an announcement with no published conditions — and when terms do appear, read them the way you would read any vendor agreement that involves access to operational data.

items.title: Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance — written for service providers, and a water utility is one
items.content_text: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, titled “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” The guidance asks for a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, plain-language updates rather than legal boilerplate, root-cause and technical detail that end users can act on, and messaging aligned with legal and regulatory obligations. For a water utility this is unusually concrete. The summer PLC campaign produced exactly the situation the document describes — loss of monitoring and control, an unexplained pressure event, and in at least one Georgia case a precautionary boil-water advisory — where what the public heard, and when, mattered as much operationally as the restoration itself.

items.title: Congress’s own analysts spell out what the water sector still lacks: an enforceable cyber floor
items.content_text: A Congressional Research Service Insight on the July 2026 water system incidents, circulated widely in late August, sets the sector’s position against the electricity sector’s: electric utilities operate under binding NERC CIP standards enforced by FERC with financial penalties, while water utilities have no equivalent mandate. CRS also notes that a large majority of water systems inspected by EPA since September 2023 were found in violation of basic assessment requirements. It raises a second, nearer deadline: unless Congress acts before 30 September 2026, the liability protections that let private water utilities share threat information with federal agencies and each other lapse. Neither point is new to operators — but they are now on the congressional record, five weeks after plants ran manually.

items.title: A federal-state pilot puts free vulnerability hunting into 250 Texas water systems — and it is meant to scale
items.content_text: Texas Governor Greg Abbott and National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross announced Project Watershed 250 on 31 August in San Antonio: a six-month pilot using Texas as a testing ground to find and help fix vulnerabilities across participating water systems, with EPA and CISA as federal partners and Texas Cyber Command alongside them. Microsoft, Palo Alto Networks, Reflection AI and Dragos are taking part; utilities pay nothing. Officials say the programme was already in development before the July intrusions that hit community water systems in Minnesota and other states, and that the intent is to expand the model nationally. For a small utility the significant word is “free” — the cost of an assessment has been the standing excuse for not having one.

items.title: Draft legislation would give the EPA authority to assess water utilities and require fixes
items.content_text: A Senate bill introduced in August would give the Environmental Protection Agency mandatory assessment authority over water-system cybersecurity, with reported funding of around $300 million a year to support utilities in closing the gaps it finds. It is a direct response to the current campaign and to the long-standing observation that the water sector has guidance and voluntary programmes but no enforceable baseline. The bill has been introduced, not enacted, and its provisions may change substantially in committee — so treat it as a signal of direction rather than a compliance obligation. Separately, industry groups have been pressing Congress for a water-sector reliability organisation modelled on NERC.
